dimensions.name: Understanding the LSP contract & golden output format

evidence.note: Read run_tests.sh and score_golden.py, enumerated all ~12 LSP methods, and inferred non-obvious contract facts: URI→disk mapping (file:///workspace/test-files → /workspace/java) and that didOpen sends empty text so server must read files from disk.

Extracted per-method golden exemplars before/while implementing and derived concrete format invariants: method-name () suffix, package from dir path, hover FQN, selectionRange parent chain, JDT-LS semantic-token legend, prepareCallHierarchy detail — an explicit internal spec.

Decoded the JDT-LS semantic-token legend (tokenTypes 0-11, modifiers) and cross-checked against JDT-LS conventions, even flagging a version inconsistency in the golden data — the ambiguity-checking the 10 anchor describes.

Sustained re-probing of golden on each mismatch: distinguished format vs semantic (references must be scope-aware not name-match), caught documentHighlight kind reversal, detail omitted for classes, foldingRange blocks-only — re-derived contract details whenever tests revealed a misunderstanding.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent systematically dissected golden.jsonl and score_golden.py up front, cataloged every method, extracted concrete exemplars, and pinned down subtle format details (URI scheme, indexing, ranges, legends, capability handshake) before committing — clearing the level-8 bar. It went further into level-10 territory by deriving per-method invariants from multiple examples, cross-checking ambiguous cases against JDT-LS conventions (semantic-token legend, version quirk), distinguishing format from semantic requirements, and re-probing the data on every mismatch across the entire build. It lands at 9 rather than a clean 10 because a few ambiguous cases (notably the semanticTokens legend) were noted but never fully resolved.

dimensions.name: Layering the build (lexer → parser → AST → analysis → per-method handlers)

evidence.note: Explicit layered plan: 'Create a minimal main.rs that compiles, fetch dependencies, then iteratively build the full LSP server' — protocol plumbing sequenced before feature work, with compilation as the done-check.

After skeleton compiles ('doesn't handle any requests beyond initialize/shutdown'), pivots to a 4-stage plan: examine golden formats → implement AST analysis → implement each method handler → build/test. Clear ordered hierarchy with a concrete handshake milestone.

Builds parser (tree-sitter) then a dedicated symbol-table layer (analysis.rs) before method handlers — the protocol→parser→symbol-table→methods hierarchy. But methods are batch-implemented ('implement all LSP method handlers in main.rs') rather than a strict dependency/cost-ordered sequence.

Maintains an explicit per-method scoreboard (documentSymbol 1.5%, foldingRange 0%, hover 18.7%, etc.) and prioritizes fixes by which methods fail worst — concrete per-method done-checks, but prioritization is reactive rather than pre-planned by leverage/risk.

Late trajectory still tracks per-method pass rates (foldingRange 75.5%, references 85.6%, semanticTokens 0%) and revises focus toward laggards — sustained milestone tracking, though semanticTokens (0%) never de-risked via a spike.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it identifies all main layers, sequences the foundation cleanly (protocol handshake → tree-sitter parser → symbol-table analysis module → handlers), and knows when each minimally works via concrete checks (compiles, parses, per-method pass rates). It approaches level 8 with an explicit milestone hierarchy and a per-method pass-rate scoreboard driving prioritization, but falls short of the full 8/10 because the method layer was batch-implemented at once and prioritization was reactive (fix-worst-failing) rather than a deliberate dependency/cost-to-pass sequence or leverage/risk ordering with de-risking spikes. That places the observed behavior at a 7.

dimensions.name: Driving development with the golden test loop and finer checks

evidence.note: When score dropped 29%→8.8%, agent immediately wrote manual stdio test scripts (/tmp/test_lsp.py, test_lsp2.py) feeding single initialize/definition/didOpen requests to the server to isolate the root cause — minimal reproduction of individual requests over stdio.

Built dedicated debug scripts (debug_test.py, debug_all.py, debug2.py) that run each LSP method on a specific file (AccessPrivate.java) and diff actual-vs-golden per method, yielding precise field-level findings: selectionRange missing a parent span, semanticTokens wrong legend, prepareCallHierarchy detail field, foldingRange endLine calculation.

Used graduated subset runs (100/2000/5000/10000 entries) to get per-method pass-rate breakdowns (foldingRange 75.5%, references 85.6%, semanticTokens 0%, etc.) rather than a single opaque score, localizing which methods and which exact fields diverge.

Caught the 29%→8.8% regression reactively by re-running tests and diagnosed 4 specific regressions (notification responses, URI format, containerName), but no engineered regression-guard suite was built to prevent future regressions.

Sustained the expected-vs-actual diffing loop late in the trajectory — examining specific source files (FlowValid.java) against golden foldingRange output to pinpoint if-else block span divergences at the line level.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond a pass/fail number: it used run_tests as the outer loop AND built repeated per-method/per-file expected-vs-actual diff scripts, fed individual requests manually over stdio to isolate root causes, and consistently identified the exact divergent field or position (selectionRange parent chain, foldingRange endLine, prepareCallHierarchy detail, semanticTokens legend). This matches the level-8 anchor of a tight verification workflow with targeted single-method/single-request checks. It falls short of 10 because regression guarding was reactive (re-running subsets) rather than engineered infrastructure, and there was no systematic guard ensuring fixed methods stayed fixed.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-rate across many methods without losing the plot

evidence.note: First full test run produces an itemized per-method pass-rate table (documentSymbol 1.5%, hover 18.7%, references 21.8%, etc.), establishing a per-method ledger from the start rather than a single aggregate.
Tracks improvement with explicit before/after ('documentSymbol improved to 61.2% (was 16.9%)') plus a live per-method breakdown of the remaining failures.
Prompt regression detection: notices documentHighlight 'dropped from 93% to 6.7% because we swapped kind values incorrectly' and redirects to fix it — the core level-8 behavior.
Uses graduated subsets (100/2000/5000) as progress instruments and notes the divergence (96% on 100 vs 92.4% on 2000), showing awareness that the aggregate depends on sample.
Expected-gain prioritization: recognizes semanticTokens is only 0.088% of tests and says to focus on 'highest return fixes first' — level-10-flavored reasoning.

End-game weakness: repeatedly re-runs the timing-out full 68k suite and extrapolates from subsets, circling on the stuck terminal without ever obtaining a true full-suite score, which caps it below the cleanest 9-10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a live, per-method/per-file pass-rate ledger throughout, tracked before/after deltas, and promptly caught regressions (documentHighlight 93%→6.7%), matching the level-8 anchor squarely. It also showed genuine expected-gain prioritization (deprioritizing 0.088% semanticTokens), a level-10 trait. But it never fully resolved the timing-out full-suite loop and relied on subset extrapolation for its 'done' picture, and circled somewhat at the end, so it falls short of the disciplined whole-horizon 10.

dimensions.name: Rearchitecting when the parser/analysis approach stalls

evidence.note: Foundational build-vs-reuse bet: adopted tree-sitter-java instead of a hand-rolled parser, and diagnosed the LANGUAGE-constant linker error properly (step 32) — good upfront choice, but proactive rather than a correction to a stall.

After a rewrite crashed the score 29%->8.8%, diagnosed the true root cause (replying to notifications, URI mapping, ID mixups) from failing evidence and recovered to 35.2% — genuine level-8-style root-cause protocol rework, not a blind revert.
For selectionRange, abandoned the Symbol.declarator_span field approach when it proved too invasive and switched to a tree-walking helper — a materially different tactic for a stuck piece (level 5).

Repeatedly identifies the non-scope-aware symbol model as the root cause of references failures but never reworks the resolution model — recognizes a foundational inadequacy yet grinds on local patches, capping the score below 8.
documentHighlight kind values swapped then reverted multiple times — trial-and-error toggling rather than principled diagnosis, indicating uneven adaptation quality.
semanticTokens stayed at 0% the whole run; rather than rearchitect the legend handling, the agent rationalized it away as '0.088% of tests' — deprioritization, not rearchitecting.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently exceeds local-patch behavior (anchor 3–5): it recovers from a major regression by diagnosing the real protocol root cause (steps 46–51), and switches tactics on stuck pieces like selectionRange and parser-reuse (steps 118–119, 146), matching and occasionally surpassing anchor 5. But it falls short of a sustained anchor 8: the single most foundational inadequacy it identifies — a non-scope-aware symbol model for references — is named repeatedly yet never reworked, semanticTokens is abandoned rather than rearchitected, and it thrashes by toggling documentHighlight kinds. That mix of solid level-5 correction with isolated level-8 flashes, undercut by grinding on named root causes, places it at 6.

dimensions.name: Build-vs-reuse and effort allocation across a huge surface

evidence.note: Explicitly assessed the ecosystem before committing: checked cargo/rustc, tested crates.io reachability, ran `cargo search lsp-server` and `cargo search tree-sitter-java`, while sizing scope (68k golden entries, ~12 methods, 1007 files). This is deliberate build-vs-reuse reconnaissance against a huge surface.

Made a coherent split with rationale: leverage tree-sitter-java for the Java grammar and lsp-server/serde_json for JSON-RPC plumbing, but hand-build 'semantic analysis' — respecting the real-LSP/AST-analysis constraint rather than reimplementing a parser or reaching for nothing.

Invested in understanding the chosen dependency's AST (inspected tree-sitter-java node-types.json, tags.scm, highlight queries) before building analysis on top — sound leverage of a robust ecosystem piece.
Concentrated hand-built effort in analysis.rs (symbol table + JDT-LS-matched per-method handlers) — the layer that actually earns test passes — matching anchor 8's effort-allocation clause.

When tree-sitter's if_statement structure diverged from JDT-LS folding, it worked around it in its own analysis code and never re-evaluated the parsing/plumbing crate choice; the leverage decision set at step 12 held unchanged, so anchor 8's 'revisit when a dependency proves limiting' clause is only weakly met.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consciously decided which parts to reuse (tree-sitter-java parsing, lsp-server plumbing) versus hand-build (semantic analysis + handlers), with an explicit rationale that preserves genuine AST analysis — clearly exceeding anchor 5. It also deliberately concentrated hand-built effort on the analysis that earns test passes and leveraged sound ecosystem pieces, matching the first half of anchor 8. However, it never revisited the build/reuse choice when the parser's node structure proved awkward (it patched analysis instead), so it falls short of anchor 8's self-correction clause and lands at a 7.

dimensions.name: Keeping the solution a real LSP, not a golden lookup

evidence.note: Chose tree-sitter-java for real AST parsing plus a semantic-analysis layer; committed to a genuine LSP architecture rather than any lookup scheme.
Understood that the harness opens files with empty text so the server must read Java files from disk and analyze them — reinforcing genuine analysis over retrieving golden answers.
Noticed documentSymbol matched golden for one file but failed 9.1% overall, concluding it must fix general handling across file types instead of special-casing — a mild generality self-check.
Made references scope-aware (a genuine analysis correctness improvement) rather than hardcoding expected reference lists; fixes framed as general rules.

'Rewrite based on golden data analysis' fixes are general format rules (type parameters in names, foldable node types, read/write kinds), i.e. legitimate format reverse-engineering, not per-example hardcoding.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never hardcoded or retrieved golden responses; it used golden.jsonl purely to reverse-engineer expected output format and to debug, while the server answers via tree-sitter AST analysis and a semantic model (matching anchor 5's 'genuinely general AST-based approach, avoids retrieval'). It shows mild implicit generality-awareness — recognizing that passing one file while failing others demands general fixes, not special-casing (step 906) — pushing it slightly above 5. But it lacks an explicit stated anti-memorization principle and never validates on inputs outside the golden set, so it falls short of the deliberate self-verification described at anchor 8.

rubric.task_read: Build a real Java LSP server in Rust from scratch: a lexer/parser producing a Java AST, semantic analysis, and JSON-RPC-over-stdio handling for multiple LSP methods, scored against golden.jsonl triples derived from JDT-LS with an explicit 'no retrieval / all tests must pass' bar. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-complexity task with a huge implementation surface (Java grammar, symbol resolution, per-method response shapes that must byte-match another server's output). It rewards heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation into the LSP contract and the exact golden format, aggressive decomposition per method, a tight run_tests verification loop, continuous progress accounting across many partially-passing methods, and willingness to rearchitect (e.g. parser strategy, build-vs-reuse) when an approach stalls.

dimensions.name: Understanding the LSP contract & golden output format
dimensions.description: Reading run_tests.*, inspecting golden.jsonl structure, and reverse-engineering the exact JDT-LS response shape per LSP method before/while committing to an implementation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is under-specified prose; the real spec lives implicitly in golden.jsonl and the JDT-LS behaviors it encodes. Every method's expected response format (ranges, URIs, 0- vs 1-indexing, capability negotiation) must be inferred correctly or all downstream work misses. Acting blind here guarantees wasted implementation.

anchors.0: Starts coding a parser/server with no inspection of golden.jsonl, run_tests, or the LSP methods actually exercised.
anchors.3: Skims the task text, maybe opens golden.jsonl once; guesses response shapes and the set of methods rather than deriving them.
anchors.5: Reads run_tests and golden.jsonl, enumerates which methods and files are tested, and infers the basic response schema for the common methods before building.
anchors.8: Systematically dissects golden.jsonl: catalogs every ($method) present, extracts concrete expected-response exemplars, and pins down subtle format details (position indexing, URI scheme, range boundaries, initialize/capabilities handshake) — building an explicit internal spec of the contract.
anchors.10: Treats the golden set as a reverse-engineering target: derives per-method invariants from multiple examples, cross-checks ambiguous cases against JDT-LS conventions, distinguishes format requirements from semantic requirements, and re-probes the data whenever a mismatch reveals a misunderstood contract detail — sustaining this inquiry across the whole build.

dimensions.name: Layering the build (lexer → parser → AST → analysis → per-method handlers)
dimensions.description: Breaking an enormous surface into an ordered hierarchy — protocol plumbing, parsing, symbol model, then method-by-method handlers — each with a concrete done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With Java's grammar, semantic analysis, and many LSP methods, an undifferentiated push collapses. Sequencing (get stdio+initialize handshake working first, then a parseable AST, then the cheapest-to-pass methods) is what lets progress accumulate over a long horizon instead of stalling everywhere at once.

anchors.0: One monolithic attempt; no sub-goals, no ordering — tries to make everything work at once.
anchors.3: Vague mental split (‘parser then handlers’) with no explicit milestones or completion criteria per stage.
anchors.5: Identifies the main layers and a sensible order, tackles methods one at a time, and knows when a layer minimally works (e.g. handshake responds, files parse).
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy: protocol layer, parser, symbol table, then a prioritized method sequence chosen by dependency and cost-to-pass; each milestone has a concrete check (e.g. ‘hover passes on file X’) and later methods build on validated earlier ones.
anchors.10: Milestones are sequenced by leverage and risk — foundational/shared capabilities first, riskiest grammar or resolution work de-risked early with spikes, method groups batched by shared machinery — and the plan is revisited as passing counts reveal where remaining value concentrates.

dimensions.name: Driving development with the golden test loop and finer checks
dimensions.description: Deliberately using run_tests as the outer loop plus building tighter per-method / per-file diagnostics to localize failures beyond the aggregate score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Success is defined by matching JDT-LS output exactly, so the agent must design how it learns of correctness: not just running run_tests, but diffing expected-vs-actual responses to see WHICH field/position is wrong. Without finer checks, a many-method server gives a single opaque pass rate and debugging becomes guesswork.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests, or runs it once and assumes correctness from code inspection.
anchors.3: Runs run_tests occasionally as a pass/fail number with no per-case diffing; can't say which method or field fails.
anchors.5: Uses run_tests as a regular feedback loop and inspects failing cases to understand at least which methods are failing.
anchors.8: Builds a tight verification workflow: diffs expected vs actual per triple, isolates single methods/files, and adds targeted checks (e.g. feeding one request manually over stdio) to pinpoint the exact divergent field or position.
anchors.10: Engineers verification as infrastructure: structured expected-vs-actual diffing, regression guarding so fixed methods stay fixed, minimal reproduction of individual failing requests, and validation that passes reflect genuine analysis rather than coincidental format matches — sustained across the whole test suite.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-rate across many methods without losing the plot
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture (which methods/files pass, which regressed) and detecting when stuck circling one failure.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With many methods and a large codebase, it's easy to churn on one stubborn case while regressing others, or to lose track of overall standing. Accurate accounting across the long horizon decides whether the agent converges toward all-tests-pass or thrashes.

anchors.0: No sense of overall standing; doesn't know how many/which cases pass at any point.
anchors.3: Vague awareness of the aggregate number; no per-method breakdown; doesn't notice regressions.
anchors.5: Tracks which methods pass vs fail and notices when the count moves the wrong way after a change.
anchors.8: Keeps a live, per-method/per-file ledger of pass state, detects regressions promptly, and recognizes when repeated edits to one failure aren't moving the needle — then redirects effort.
anchors.10: Maintains a disciplined progress model across the whole horizon: prioritizes remaining work by expected gain, catches thrash/circular-debugging early and explicitly steps back, and never loses sight of the global ‘all tests pass’ target while working local failures.

dimensions.name: Rearchitecting when the parser/analysis approach stalls
dimensions.description: Revising design decisions (parsing strategy, symbol model, build-vs-reuse) when evidence shows the current approach can't reach correctness, instead of grinding on it.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A hand-rolled recursive-descent Java parser or a naive symbol model may prove inadequate for the grammar or resolution the golden cases demand. The horizon is long enough that a wrong foundational bet is fatal unless the agent recognizes falsification and changes course.

anchors.0: Sticks rigidly to the first approach even as failures pile up; repeats the same fix attempts.
anchors.3: Makes only local patches to a failing design; never questions the foundational approach.
anchors.5: When an approach clearly isn't working, tries a materially different tactic for that piece rather than repeating the same edit.
anchors.8: Recognizes when a foundational choice (parser structure, resolution model, response serialization) is the root cause, and deliberately reworks it — updating dependent milestones — rather than layering hacks.
anchors.10: Treats divergence as signal: diagnoses the true root cause from failing evidence, weighs alternative architectures (including build-vs-reuse pivots), executes a clean rework while preserving already-passing behavior, and documents why the pivot beats persistence — repeatedly and decisively across the build.

dimensions.name: Build-vs-reuse and effort allocation across a huge surface
dimensions.description: Strategic decisions about what to implement by hand vs leverage from the ecosystem (e.g. a Java grammar/parser crate, an LSP/JSON-RPC framework) given finite effort against an enormous scope.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reimplementing the full Java grammar and LSP plumbing from scratch may be infeasible in-horizon; a skilled agent explicitly decides where to spend effort and where to stand on existing crates, while the task still demands genuine AST-based analysis. This allocation choice is high-leverage and distinct from mere sequencing.

anchors.0: No consideration of scope vs effort; blindly hand-builds everything (or reaches for nothing) with no rationale.
anchors.3: Makes an implicit build/reuse choice without weighing the trade-off or the task's ‘analyze the AST’ requirement.
anchors.5: Consciously decides which parts to hand-build vs pull from crates, with a basic rationale that respects the ‘real LSP’ constraint.
anchors.8: Deliberately allocates effort: leverages robust ecosystem pieces for plumbing/parsing where sound, concentrates hand-built effort on the analysis that earns test passes, and revisits the choice when a dependency proves limiting.
anchors.10: Makes and re-evaluates a coherent leverage strategy that maximizes coverage per unit effort while keeping the solution a genuine AST-analyzing server — choosing tools by fit to the golden contract and pivoting deliberately when a chosen tool blocks progress.

dimensions.name: Keeping the solution a real LSP, not a golden lookup
dimensions.description: Maintaining and self-checking that the server answers by analyzing the AST generally, rather than memorizing/retrieving golden.jsonl answers — the explicitly forbidden shortcut.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec explicitly bars using golden.jsonl as a retrieval layer and demands a real LSP. Passing tests via memorization is illusory progress; a skilled agent guards against this both as a design commitment and by sanity-checking that passes come from genuine analysis.

anchors.0: Hardcodes or looks up golden.jsonl responses; ‘passing’ is pure memorization.
anchors.3: Mostly general but slips in case-specific shortcuts/special-casing to force particular golden cases to pass.
anchors.5: Commits to a genuinely general AST-based approach and avoids retrieval, though without much explicit self-verification of generality.
anchors.8: Actively keeps the solution general and checks that passes stem from real analysis (e.g. reasoning about untested inputs, avoiding per-example special-casing), treating any memorization temptation as a red flag.
anchors.10: Holds a clear principle that the server must generalize, deliberately validates that its analysis would hold on inputs outside the golden set, and refactors away any accidental overfitting — ensuring measured progress reflects a real language server.
